record.original_question: For theta in (0, pi), let V_theta = {r e^{it} : r > 0, |t| > theta}. If L(V) denotes the Lehmer-Langevin constant of an open set V, compute L(V_theta) explicitly as a function of theta.

evidence.quote: Problem 4.6. For θ ∈ (0, π), define Vθ = {reit ; r > 0, |t| > θ}. Compute L(Vθ ) in terms of θ.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
For an open set $V \subset \mathbb{C}^*$, define the Lehmer–Langevin constant
$$L(V) = \liminf_{\alpha} M(\alpha)^{1/\deg(\alpha)},$$
where the liminf is taken over nonzero algebraic numbers $\alpha$ which are not roots of unity, all of whose Galois conjugates lie outside $V$, and $M(\alpha)$ denotes the Mahler measure of the minimal polynomial of $\alpha$ over $\mathbb{Z}$.

For each $\theta \in (0,\pi)$, let
$$V_\theta = \{\, r e^{it} : r > 0,\ |t| > \theta \,\} \subset \mathbb{C}^*$$
denote the complement (in $\mathbb{C}^*$) of the closed sector of half-angle $\theta$ about the positive real axis.

Determine $L(V_\theta)$ as an explicit function of $\theta \in (0,\pi)$.
artifact.status_search_result: Langevin proved that $L(V_\theta) > 1$ for all $\theta \in (0,\pi)$, and Rhin–Smyth determined the exact value of this constant on nine subintervals of $[0, 2\pi/3]$. They conjectured the function is a decreasing staircase function with only finitely many discontinuities on any compact subinterval of $[0,\pi)$. The function has been further refined on additional subintervals by Rhin–Wu and others, but a complete explicit formula for all $\theta \in (0,\pi)$ remains unknown.

status_evidence.title: On the Absolute Mahler Measure of Polynomials Having All Zeros in a Sector
status_evidence.snippet: Rhin and Smyth determined exact value of c(θ) for θ in nine subintervals of [0,120°] and conjectured a staircase structure.
status_evidence.claim: The function L(V_θ) (equivalently c(θ)) is known explicitly only on certain subintervals; a full formula is conjectural.

status_evidence.title: The Mahler measure of algebraic numbers: a survey (Smyth)
status_evidence.snippet: Langevin's theorem states c(θ) > 1; Rhin–Smyth made it effective on subintervals of [0,180°).
status_evidence.claim: The exact value is not known for all θ; the question is partially answered.
